analysis.one_liner: Let the president wiretap suspected terrorists' communications without a court order, in renewable 45-day periods.
analysis.headline: The Senate Judiciary Committee reported the bill to the floor in September 2006, but it never received a vote before the 109th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would write into law a president's power to run electronic surveillance of suspected terrorists without first getting a court order, replacing the standing requirement that the government get a warrant from the secret foreign intelligence court. Each surveillance program would run for 45 days at a time, renewed on the president's say-so, with classified reports to small intelligence subcommittees instead of any judicial check. It would also make it a crime, punishable by up to 15 years in prison or a $1,000,000 fine, for anyone authorized to know about such surveillance to disclose it.
analysis.who_benefits: If it passed, the president and intelligence agencies would gain standing legal authority to intercept communications without a court order, and telecommunications carriers ordered to help would get statutory cover and secrecy protection for that assistance.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The executive branch and phone companies

how_it_helps.text: Lets the president authorize electronic surveillance without a court order for 45-day periods when he determines it is necessary to protect the United States and there is probable cause a target is tied to a listed terrorist organization [S4]

Requires telecommunications carriers to furnish the information and technical assistance the government needs for the surveillance, with records kept under security procedures approved by the Attorney General [S4]
Creates dedicated intelligence subcommittees with expert staff to monitor the program and requires semiannual classified reports on surveillance of targets inside the United States [S4]

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people communicating with parties overseas could have their calls and emails intercepted without any warrant or judge, and oversight would be classified reports to a handful of members rather than court review.

drawbacks.text: Renewal of each 45-day surveillance period rests on the president's own determination and the Attorney General's review, not on any court, so a program could continue indefinitely without judicial approval [S4]

It would create a crime carrying up to 15 years in prison or a $1,000,000 fine for unauthorized disclosure of information about the program — or about any FISA surveillance program — which would chill the whistleblowing and press reporting that exposed the underlying warrantless program in the first place [S4]

Communications could be swept in whenever one party appears to be outside the United States, meaning calls and emails between people in the U.S. and people abroad could be collected without individualized warrants [S4]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers real counterterrorism tools, but the trade it asks for is lopsided: it swaps a court order requirement that has applied to foreign intelligence surveillance since 1978 for presidential self-certification, policed only by classified reports to a few members of Congress. The stiff criminal penalty for disclosure would make it harder for the public to ever learn what the program does. An honest supporter would call this a genuine oversight improvement over no law at all; an honest critic would note that the constitutionally questionable practice it legalized was already underway.

outcome.mechanism: The Judiciary Committee reported it favorably and put it on the Senate calendar in September 2006, but no senator ever voted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced March 16, 2006 by Senator DeWine with three Republican cosponsors, and referred to the Judiciary Committee [S1]
Held two rounds of hearings in July and August 2006, then reported without amendment on September 13, 2006 and placed on the Senate calendar under General Orders [S6]
The Senate never took it up; it sat on the calendar until the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007, so it died without a floor vote [S6]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the warrant requirement of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act stayed in place as written law, and the executive branch did not get a statute authorizing surveillance without court orders. Ordinary people who make calls or send emails to people overseas are better off than they would have been under it; the penalty provision that would have punished disclosures about surveillance programs also never became law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People whose communications stayed under warrant law

for.name: Sen. Mike DeWine
for.role: U.S. Senator from Ohio, bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and steered it through the Judiciary Committee

for.name: Sens. Lindsey Graham, Chuck Hagel, and Olympia Snowe
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as original supporters

for.name: Sen. Arlen Specter
for.what_they_did: Held hearings and reported the bill to the Senate without amendment

for.name: President George W. Bush
for.what_they_did: Had been running warrantless surveillance through the NSA since 2001 and pressed Congress to give it legal footing; the bill would have done so

against.name: Senate leadership of both parties
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor for a vote before the Congress ended

against.name: Civil liberties groups
against.role: Advocacy organizations opposing surveillance without court orders
against.what_they_did: Opposed legislation that would ratify warrantless wiretapping rather than require judicial warrants

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, and no Democrat signed on; the bill never reached a roll call.

industries.note: The bill would legally require phone and internet companies to help the government intercept communications and would keep their assistance secret under security procedures. Their customers would have no way to know their calls were being turned over without a warrant.

industries.industry: Federal intelligence agencies and the executive branch
industries.note: Would convert the warrantless surveillance program revealed in 2005 into standing statutory authority, renewable indefinitely by the president without a judge. The public would get classified reports to a few members of Congress instead of court review.

industries.industry: Government employees, contractors, and journalists handling surveillance information
industries.note: New criminal penalties of up to 15 years and $1,000,000 for unauthorized disclosure would fall on people inside the system and on anyone they tell. Ordinary people lose a channel for learning what is done in their name.
